messages.author: 90589675ea303876
messages.subject: GWAS-by-subtraction
parts:
Hi all, first I just wanted to thank you for the detailed wiki and tutorials allowing me to easily follow your methods. Even though I have only a basic knowledge of R and SEM I was able to follow and run your scripts with ease. I was delighted to come across the recent pre-print  of your GWAS-by-subtraction (GBS) in bioRxiv as I was looking for a way to perform this on my data.

To keep it simple I have a GWAS that measures RV and one that measures V (both from subsets of the UK biobank) and I want to generate a GWAS of R without the V component. What I did before I found this method was to simple take all SNPs that were significant in RV (<5e -8) but not significant in V (>.05) to bring forward for investigation. I easily fitted my data into the model presented in your tutorial and generated a GWAS for R however your method is much more conservative (and robust) and I just have a couple of questions.

The following are some examples from my data running GBS on chromosome 1( the GBS results are highlighted in yellow and the other results are from my original GWAS)

 
GWAS SNP A2 A1 or/est   P
V rs12410444 A G or 1.063 6.88E-15
RV A G or 1.039 3.29E-07
R   A G est 0.011 0.919202
V rs60482554 T A or 1.039 4.91E-06
RV T A or 1.004 5.91E-01
R   T A est 0.011 0.059807
V rs12735232 T C or 1.015 1.30E-01
RV T C or 1.085 2.60E-18
R   T C est 0.013 9.23E-10
V rs847705 A G or 1.011 3.01E-01
RV A G or 1.049 4.96E-06
R   G A est 0.015 0.001335

I was just looking for a possible explanation for the large increase in p value from RV to R where V is not significant in the third example (rs12735232)  and the flipping in the fourth example (rs847705).

Thanks again for sharing this method.

All the best Joan

messages.author: 3b39745f73eec779
messages.subject: Re: GWAS-by-subtraction
parts:
HI Joan,

Glad you found our tutorial good to follow along. To judge whether these results are inconsistent I would need to see the rest of the model parameters you estimated. So I suggest running the models without a SNP, and reporting back to us with the output. What I would also need is the other SNP estimate from genomic SEM (the effect on V).

Based on what you present now the 3th example seems reasonable, the change in p-value is consistent with a ±2.6 SD change in parameter estimate, here I compute the Z values (estimate/se) from the p-values:

> qnorm(2.60E-18,lower.tail = F)
[1] 8.648896
> qnorm(9.23E-10,lower.tail = F)
[1] 6.010809

The change is sort of consistent with the % change on log(oddsratio) you observe from RV (or 1.015) to V (or 1.085):


> log(1.015)/log(1.085)
[1] 0.1825032
> (8.648896-6.010809) /8.648896
[1] 0.3050201

Its not exactly the same but since the GWAS of R and RV are from the same cohort, and I assume the traits are correlated, its not unsurprising that the standard erros (and thus p-values) are correlated, this is also reflected int the p-value of the final estimate.

Anyway this is just some first pass intuitions hope they help.

Best,
Michel
 





Best,
Michel

messages.author: 3b39745f73eec779
messages.subject: Re: GWAS-by-subtraction
parts:
Hi Joan,

Your model makes sense, what flipped the signs on est? a code change? Did the loadings flip to negative? The model (without the SNP) is identical regardless of whether the loading are negative or positive, what you want to avoid is the model randomly flipping the signs on the loadings and therefore the SNP effects. Doe that make sense to you?

Now in terms of evaluating the results how about you use either GenomicSEM or LDscore regression to estimate the SNP heritability of you var and res GWASes? Perhaps you (like we did) have external traits for which you have prior expectations about the genetic correlation with R and V? Those can help you figure out whether the result is as expected. 


Best,
Michel

messages.author: d6d83e22ef3ba9f1
messages.subject: Re: GWAS-by-subtraction
parts:
Hi Joan, 

The output from the GWAS commands should match with respect to number of SNPs with output from the sumstats file. For runs that did not converge, or failed in some way, the function should print rows with those warnings and error messages so even in these cases you should have ended up with 8378151 SNPs. If you are running the multivariate GWAS using serial processing, the functions will print intermittent updates with respect to what model it is on (e.g., "Running Model 10,000) for every 1,000 runs. If you are using parallel processing, unfortunately the package doesn't print any updates at the current moment because the different cores may be on different runs and you would just end up getting a bunch of garbled output the way things are currently coded. Are you using serial or parallel processing?  

On the computer clusters I use, if the cluster runs out of memory the job will typically fail without saving any of the output, so I've also never run into a situation where it saves partial output at the point it runs out of memory. However, this could be a cluster specific feature so running out of memory seems like a likely explanation. Since all multivariate GWAS runs are entirely independent of one another, my suggestion would be to split up the output from sumstats in some way (by chromosome, or in even chunks) and try re-running to see if the output ends early, or the same SNPs are excluded from your output. 

Best,
-Andrew

Hi Joan,

to add to what Andrew has said some debugging tips: I would try the following, run 1000 SNPs to make sure it does actually give you a 1000 results (this should be well within memory for any machine). If it does your then reasonable sure the problem is memory. trying to run very memory heavy tasks in parrallel is also extra slow as the R workspace is copied for each core I think.

I agree with Andree for best performance run per chromosome,  half a chromosome, or ecen sized chunks. This should speed up your analysis 22x or even 44x if you have the server nodes available.

Best,
Michel

messages.author: d6d83e22ef3ba9f1
messages.subject: Re: GWAS-by-subtraction
parts: Were you running the full sample of SNPs in parallel? That would explain it since parallel processing chunks the runs across cores, and if certain runs within a core finish-up before your memory issues kick in you would end up with a somewhat random assortment of SNPs in your output. Still not something I've personally seen happen, but again you may have a specific cluster environment that is operating differently in terms of how it handles memory issues. If you weren't running in parallel we may need to do some more digging. Might be worth also specifically picking out 1000 snps that were not in in the output of 3.2 million SNPs to make sure that selected subset runs ok...
